meta.description: Not Oscar Wilde. The line surfaces as a 1955 Broadway wisecrack in Walter Winchell's column; the Wilde credit appears only in 1989, unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'True friends stab you in the front'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it under Disputed: earliest known example is Walter Winchell's column, mid-January 1955. Wilde died in 1900.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — an unsourced mid-century wisecrack
answer.authorDates: First recorded mid-January 1955 · Broadway wisecrack quoted by Walter Winchell
answer.sourceLine: No work of Wilde’s contains this line, and he died in 1900. Wikiquote files it under Disputed and gives the earliest known example as Walter Winchell’s syndicated column of mid-January 1955, reporting a Broadway gag; the first credit to Wilde it can find is a 1989 book, offered with no source.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

source.excerpt: On Broadway, cynically reports Jimmy Nelson, “a true friend is one who stabs you in the front”
trail: Mid-January 1955 — the first known appearance is a Broadway gag in Walter Winchell’s syndicated column: “On Broadway, cynically reports Jimmy Nelson, ‘a true friend is one who stabs you in the front’”, as transcribed by Wikiquote ↗. Note that even here Winchell is relaying it as something already in circulation.

1958 to 1984 — the quip keeps changing hands. Wikiquote records ↗ a 1958 version credited to actor Steve Dunne, a 1981 version credited to writer-producer Leonard Levinson — in Gus McLeavy’s The Bathroom Almanac ↗ — and a 1984 Ms. Magazine piece calling it simply the Hollywood definition of a friend.

1989 — the earliest credit to Wilde that Wikiquote can find, in the form “A good friend is one who stabs you in the front”, appears in Thomas R. Whissen’s The Devil’s Advocates: Decadence in Modern Literature (1989) ↗. No source is given for the attribution.
Today — the polished expansion “A true friend stabs you in the front, not the back” circulates on Goodreads under Wilde’s name ↗, still with no work, page or date attached to it.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗, which cites a scan of the Pharos-Tribune (Logansport, Indiana) for 16 January 1955. That scan is paywalled and we could not open it, so this is Wikiquote’s reading of the column, not ours.
source.rightsNote: We make no rights claim for this wording. It cannot be tied to any identifiable authored work: the earliest record is a 1955 newspaper column relaying an already-circulating Broadway quip, and the popular modern form is a later expansion of unknown authorship. Because nothing here is pinned to a specific pre-1931 publication, this line must not be treated as public domain on the strength of Wilde’s name.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: Why the line lands on Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Wilde was an Irish poet, playwright and critic whose comedies — Lady Windermere’s Fan, An Ideal Husband, The Importance of Being Earnest — and his one novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray, made him the most quotable writer of the Victorian era. He died in Paris on 30 November 1900. Precisely because his real epigrams are compressed, cynical and inverted, almost any clever reversal now gets pinned to him, and this friendship line is one of the most travelled examples.

misattribution.heading: Who has been credited — and why none of it holds
misattribution.intro: This is a quote that has been handed round like a hat. In the thirty-four years between its first recorded appearance and its first Wilde credit, it was pinned on at least three different people, none of them with a source. Wilde was simply the name that finally stuck.

items.why: Wilde died in Paris on 30 November 1900 ↗, more than fifty years before the saying is first recorded. Wikiquote places it in the Disputed section ↗ and reports that the earliest attribution to him is from 1989, with no source given.

Before Wilde’s name was attached, Wikiquote records ↗ a 1958 version credited to actor Steve Dunne and a 1981 version — “He is a fine friend. He stabs you in the front” — credited to Hollywood writer and producer Leonard Levinson. Neither credit comes with a source either; the pattern is a floating gag looking for an owner.

By 1984, per Wikiquote ↗, a Ms. Magazine article was presenting it not as anyone’s line but as an industry saying — a friend being “someone who stabs you in the front.” That is what an orphaned wisecrack looks like just before a famous name adopts it.

items.who: “A true friend stabs you in the front, not the back”
items.why: The tidier, more explanatory version now shared most widely — for example on Goodreads under Wilde’s name ↗ — is longer than any of the recorded mid-century forms and carries no book or page at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: this is an anonymous mid-twentieth-century show-business wisecrack, first recorded in Walter Winchell’s column in mid-January 1955 ↗, that did not acquire Oscar Wilde’s name until 1989.

context.heading: What Wilde actually said about friends and enemies
lead: Wilde is one of the internet’s two or three great attribution magnets, and this line is a textbook case of why. It has the shape of a Wilde epigram — a moral inversion delivered flat, turning “stabbed in the back” inside out so that brutal honesty becomes the mark of real friendship. It is genuinely good. It simply is not his.

The paper trail runs the other way round. The saying first surfaces in mid-twentieth-century American show business, drifts between named comedians and writers for thirty years without settling on any of them, and only picks up Wilde’s name in 1989 — at which point the name sticks, because a name sells a quote. What Wilde really wrote on the subject is sharper and stranger: in The Picture of Dorian Gray ↗, Lord Henry announces that he chooses his friends for their good looks, his acquaintances for their good characters, and his enemies for their good intellects — “A man cannot be too careful in the choice of his enemies.”
detailsBody: The 1955 Winchell citation comes from Wikiquote, which transcribes the column line and cites a scan of the Pharos-Tribune (Logansport, Indiana) hosted on Newspapers.com. That scan sits behind a paywall and returned a 403 to us, so we have not independently inspected the printed page; we are relying on Wikiquote’s transcription and flagging that honestly rather than presenting the newspaper as something we read.

The two Google Books items Wikiquote cites we did check directly: the 1981 volume is Gus McLeavy’s The Bathroom Almanac, and the 1989 volume that first attaches Wilde’s name is Thomas R. Whissen’s The Devil’s Advocates: Decadence in Modern Literature. Quote Investigator, which normally handles quotes of this profile, has never published on this one — so Wikiquote’s Disputed entry is the best research available, and we do not claim anything beyond it.
context.pull: A man cannot be too careful in the choice of his enemies.
